utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated, sir. Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. At the very outset, I will inform you briefly of the proceedings we will implement during your testimony. You asked for protective measures, which were approved by the Trial Chamber: image distortion, voice distortion and a pseudonym. During these proceedings, I will address you as Mr. MM-117 or Witness. Is that all right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, I will now show you a document containing your personal details, your pseudonym and the fact that you are a witness. Please read it silently to yourself and just tell us whether the details on this document correspond to your personal details. Don't read it out loud. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have a copy for our learned friends and I do apologise for not providing it immediately. Your Honours, I tender this document with the witness's pseudonym under seal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. The document is admitted under seal. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number 964, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please, please let us both bear in mind that we have to make a pause between my question and your answer so that the interpreters can do their job, and I would also like to ask you to give me direct answers to my questions. If there is any need to explain things, I will put another question to you. Also, please speak slowly and bear in mind that when you mention the offices you held or the jobs you held, not to describe this in detail, just mention, "My job" for example without specifying it. If there is any need to specify any of these details which might identify you, the Defence will ask for us to pass into private session and then we will be able to talk about this. Do you understand this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Did you go to primary and secondary school in your place of birth?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us where you went to university and what you studied?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: The faculty of political sciences in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: After graduating from the faculty of political sciences, what job did you do? You don't have to mention the institution where you worked.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: I was an assistant lecturer in a school and at the university.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: It seems my microphone was not switched on. I don't know if my question was heard. Oh, yes. It's all right. Thank you. What year did you graduate in?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So from the time you graduated from university to 1991, you were a lecturer, is this correct, a university lecturer and a lecturer at institutions of higher education?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think we should move into private session to avoid identifying the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: At one point you said that in 1991 you left Zagreb. Did you have problems? What was the main reason you left Zagreb? Can we clarify that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: The main reason was my feeling of being physically imperilled and my inability to find work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say you felt physically under threat, are you speaking of personal danger?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you explain to us how this feeling of personal danger arose?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Well, I would have to explain at length by your leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: After the elections held in May 1990 in the former Yugoslavia, there was change of government in most republics and the political climate in Croatia and in Zagreb where I was living changed. My predominant feeling was the following. I had been living in Zagreb for a full 15 years up to that point. I had lived well. I was a citizen like every other citizen in Zagreb and Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please excuse me for interrupting you but I will ask you -- I'm sorry for interrupting your natural rhythm. If you can slow down for the sake of the interpreters, they haven't complained, but if you can speak a little slower it will be easier for them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: I will try. I do tend to speak fast and I too apologise. Up to 1990, when elections were held in Croatia, I was a citizen like any other, but a little before that date, and after that date, during the pre-election campaign, the situation changed, and I no longer felt as simply a citizen but I felt that society and the new state were identifying me as a Serb not simply a citizen. So that although up to that point, I hardly was aware that I was a Serb because of the way I was raised in my family, I came to understand through the attitude of the Croatian government that I was a Serb. These are hard words but they are true. I still have many friends in Zagreb and Croatia but the state system was carrying out repression in politics and in the media and for this reason, most of the people accepted this logic. Specifically, in mid-1991 or rather in early 1991, in February or March, I was approached by a man in Frankopanska street in Zagreb. I was just about to board a tram. And he told me that my neck was good for hanging from a lamp post.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Witness. Did you know this person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I don't know the reason for which he established that I was a Serb but he approached me and that's what he said and then he entered the tram with me. I was going to the republic square which is now called the Ban Jelacic square. There were a lot of passengers in the tram. He wouldn't stop shouting at me. No one paid any attention or no one had the strength to say anything against him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: That was in the morning, in the afternoon, in the evening? When was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: It was in the afternoon, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This was taking place in the centre of the town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Yes, in the very centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that after what he had said in the street, this man entered the tram with you and he shouted at you. What was it that he was saying to you when you said no one opposed him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Well, he said I was a member of the military, that Zagreb wasn't a place for me to live in, I should move, I'd be swallowed up by the night. I would just disappear. I can't remember everything else he said but it went on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: How did this meeting end in the tram?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: At the next stop, I got out, at trg Republika, at the public square. But that was just one event among many such events in that nightmare situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness are you saying there were similar events? You said that was just one event. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Well, I had other unpleasant experiences. I was threatened on other occasions in this way. In my flat in Zagreb, I have two-room flat in Zagreb, fully furnished. Eggs were thrown at the door on a number of occasions. I received messages saying that I had to move out, and similarly, on two occasions, sometime in August or September, 1991, my wheel, my car wheel was unscrewed. This was done to Serbs quite frequently at the time. I tried to check this every morning. And this was a sign telling me that I had to leave Zagreb, although at that time I was in an organisation with other prominent individuals and we tried to resolve the Serbian issue in Croatia in a peaceful way but I wouldn't speak about this now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we just briefly move into private session, into closed session, so that the witness can tell us which organisation he was a member of?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you mentioned those unpleasant experiences that you had had. You said that there were a number of such experiences that you had and you described them. Do you know who the perpetrators were, who was throwing these eggs at your door, who unscrewed your car wheel? Do you know these people? Personally, did you ever find out about their identity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I couldn't carry out such an investigation either but as an analyst, what I did know was that the system was behind all of this and I can confirm this claim by providing you with the following examples. The well known poet and philosopher Goethe said on one occasion that if you treat the people as if they were stupid, they really will act stupidly. He said that stupidity is a disease against which one has to fight. The authorities in Croatia treated the people as if they were stupid and this was a self-fulfilling prophecy. I'll provide you with two or three obvious examples. Mr. Sime Djodan, deputy of Mr. Tudjman's, a deputy of the president of Croatia, at the Alka in Sinj, the games in Sinj in August 1991 said in public and on television, and he was addressing the Serbs in a threatening manner, he said that the Serbs should take care because on average they were 15 centimetres shorter than the Croats and they had cone-like heads. He also said that their brains were probably smaller than Croatian brains. This was said on television. This was at a public meeting, at an assembly. And naturally, this involved racial discrimination. This also confirms the scenario that as early as 1990 at a meeting of the HDZ, the president of the HDZ, Mr. Tudjman, later to become the president, said that NDH, the Independent State of Croatia which was based on a fascist ideology, was the historical objective of the Croatian people. Then there are these personal experiences of mine. Well you've asked me whether I knew the identities of the individuals who created certain acts. I'm saying the system was behind it and this is also obvious because on the 2nd of May 1991, in Zadar, over 120 Serbian catering establishments were damaged and in a period of about a month about a thousand buildings were destroyed in that area. This was called -- so-called crystal night.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When these unpleasant events happened, were you involved in politics or were you publicly engaged? Were you a well known individual for the public?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: No. I wasn't involved in politics apart from the fact that I was a member of the organisation that I have already mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was there a reason for anyone to treat you in this way, to persecute you in this way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: I'm certain that given that I was brought up to believe in the idea of Yugoslavia, given the way I acted, there was no one who would want to harm me, but I was someone from a people who was treated by the Croatian authorities as a negative element. And that's why I was treated the way I was treated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you mentioned your experiences. Those are the experiences of one individual. Were there other individuals of Serbian nationality in Croatia who had similar experiences at the time? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Well, it's a well known fact, and naturally I'm familiar with quite a few examples. I should point out that in 1993, Mr. Akashi stated in one of his documents that in 1990 and 1991, over 250.000 inhabitants had been driven out of towns in Croatia. That number of individuals couldn't have had enemies, or rather, they were treated as enemies only by the system.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting you. You said 250.000 people were expelled from towns or urban areas in Croatia. What was their nationality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Serbs. I'm talking about Serbs alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You've been explaining your position in Zagreb, the position that others were in, and you said, to paraphrase you, that the Croatian state was behind this. How did you arrive at this conclusion? What was happening in 1990 and 1991? What led you to believe that this was the case? What led you to this conclusion? What sort of political processes were involved? That's what I'm asking you about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Hasn't he answered that question, Mr. Milovancevic? I thought he said to us that he concluded that because of what was said by some Croatian leader in -- on television on a public platform, that Serbs have on average 15 centimetres shorter than Croats and that they've got smaller brains. That's how he explained that. Or do you want something more?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think the witness mentioned an example that is perhaps an extreme example. I'm interested in the policies and the general situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But he was answering specifically that question, how do you conclude that the state of Croatia was behind the personal experiences that you went through? And that's how he explained it. I'm trying to get us moving so that we don't repeat the same thing over and over again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm bearing that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned your personal experience and your own attitude. You told us about what these acts meant to you. What sort of conclusions could the Serbian population draw on the basis of political meetings, pre-electoral campaigns and on the basis of acts committed after the elections? Could you provide us with some brief explanations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Well, one would want to provide very lengthy explanations about these things. I'll say that given the Croatian constitution, at the end of 1990, the position of the Serbian people changed. They were no longer a constituent people, they were a national minority, and if you have a look at this within the historical context of the Second World War, this was a sort of warning issued to the Serbs. Representatives of political power adopted such a position. If representatives of a political power is speaking that means the state is speaking. I listened to what the state said. I tried to remain in Zagreb and I remained there until September of 1991. But as my security really was at risk I decided to leave Zagreb. That became obvious. And there is one other issue that is of great importance. I believe the Chamber will be interested in this too. It was the end of 1991, Croatia passed a law on distributing flats abandoned by Serbs. These flats were distributed to members of Croatian military formations. I think they were even distributed to the Ministry of Defence. This decision was taken not because there were very few flats but because many Serbs had previously left the area and thus it was necessary for the Croatian state to regulate the issue in their own way. And they wanted to distribute the flats abandoned by Serbs, including myself, to others. A tragical consequence of that law is that certain processes had been rendered legal. Many people were allowed to exert pressure on other Serbs so that they could enter into their flats in this way because if you pass a law that makes it possible to temporarily distribute flats, well, that means that you're issuing a signal for others to exert pressure on other Serbs so that they could move into their flats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, you said that you had a fully furnished flat and that you had to leave Zagreb because your life was at threat. What happened to your flat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: It is still in Croatia. I don't know what happened to it. I never had the possibility of getting it back because the Croatian state passed a law according to which over 20.000 socially-owned flats couldn't be returned to those who had lived in them. So I could not get my flat back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: May I get to that question. You said you had a fully-furnished flat. You said, Mr. Witness, you also said, I had -- or I have - it says in the transcript - "two rooms flat in Zagreb." What do you mean by "have"? Is this private ownership or is it a rented flat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was the property of the company that I worked for. It was given to me and my family and although we were not de facto the owners of the flat, the flat in a certain sense belonged to the person it had been allocated to. That's how things functioned in a socialist society. I don't know how necessary it is to go into explanations. I had furnished the flat. I don't believe it's necessary to give you a list of the furniture. The property was my own property or -- in the flat, when I left Zagreb, in September I drove through Hungary and I was only able to take my personal affairs with me, the bed, the television, the fridge and other items remained in the flat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. And you didn't get any compensation for what you left there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, never.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In connection with the rally mentioned by His Honour Judge Hoepfel, could you explain this in a different way? How were the housing problems of citizens in the Republic of Croatia resolved before 1991? I'm speaking of all citizens, and was the situation the same in all republics, when it comes to ownership of flats? Can you tell us this? Were citizens owners of their flats? Was there another way this was done?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Citizens were not owners of flats in the land registers but every citizen was allocated a flat and it was considered to be that person's flat until the end of his life and his family had the right to inherit the flat. So de facto, legally, it wasn't one won proper ownership but the flats in fact belonged to the people living in them. The reason for this was that all the citizens of the former Yugoslavia, not Croatia, contributed the money for the building of those flats. They were not bought by individuals, they were bought by society. But de facto a flat belonged to the person it was allocated to and no one could confiscate it, neither the company nor the state that had given the person the flat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said you left Zagreb because you felt physically at threat, and that you went to Knin. Where did you live in Knin? You don't have to tell us the address. Where did you live before you got the job there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you want to go into private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that the witness could answer this question without identifying his identity very briefly, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I returned to Knin because I was born in Knin. My parents were there. We had property there. And that was the only reason I returned to Knin. I engaged in farming activities and tried to find a place for myself in my new environment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we now move into private session so key can be more specific?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you explained that you accepted this new job. Can you tell us briefly what your task was? You don't have to mention the name of the institution, if possible, of course. If you need to mention it, we will move back into private session.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: In the first period, as is normal, I tried to gain an insight into the situation in the organisation I was now working in, and then I took measures to improve the personnel structure of the organisation I was in. This was done in the following way. I tried to get as many professionals who had been properly trained in internal affairs in the former Yugoslavia and in Croatia to take over responsible positions. My primary motive was to have professionals doing these jobs, and to remove those who had been appointed to their jobs for "their merit", which wasn't really professional. That was why people in Knin referred to me as an HDZ staff member who was working not in the interests of the Serb people but in the interests of the Croatian state. For this reason, some groups planned my liquidation. However, I saw in this confirmation that the policy of creating an efficient organisation, which I was trying to create with the support of Minister Martic, was something I should adhere to and insist on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you want to tell us that carrying out what you had agreed with Mr. Martic came up against resistance? Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Yes. There was a lot of resistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: While doing that job, did you have the support of Mr. Martic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Absolutely. I had his absolute support in being persistent in cleansing the personnel within the organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us briefly how the organisation of the Secretariat of the Interior on the territory of the Republic of Krajina was organised? There was the SUP in Knin?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry to do this to you but can I just ask a question before he deals with this one? Related to what he has just said. I just want to find out from whom you experienced this resistance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] History shows that in all turbulent times - just one minute, please, Your Honours, one sentence - in all times of upheaval, very often people of poor moral quality come to the surface, people protecting a certain nation, in this case the Serb nation, and they are not recognised as such at the outset, and yet they feel they have certain rights. It was very difficult to get rid of these bad people who thought they had an eternal right to remain where they were, so that in the initial phase, and even later, it's difficult to recognise who is good and who is bad. I recognised certain people as not being able to carry out their jobs professionally, in a professional manner, but they interpreted it as my protecting the interests of Croatia rather than the interests of the Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you have told us about people who were not professional. I just want to know, when I say from whom, was it from the general public in Knin, was it from the people -- the staff that was working under you? Was it a trade union? That's all I want to know. Who resisted you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand the question, Your Honours. I only worked in that organisation, and I'm referring to people who worked in that organisation, people who were below me and who felt their positions were at threat and that's why certain actions were taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: These were people of Serb extraction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, exclusively Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, in addition to the Knin SUP, Secretariat of the Interior, which other organisational units were in existence, where and where, which were covered by the Knin SUP?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: The SUP was responsible for southern Dalmatia. They had public security stations or police stations in Benkovac, Drnis, in Knin, that's where the headquarters of the SUP were located, but there was a particular public security station Benkovac, Drnis, Knin and Obrovac, as I have said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who the commander of the police station in Benkovac was and were any changes made there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Yes. But perhaps we should deal with this in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you for saying that. Your Honours, could we move into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Please continue, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: In the Benkovac area, there were certain negative phenomena, some groups appeared, and they wanted to decide about how people were to live in that area. There were some groups of people who wanted to spread fear and insecurity for all citizens who lived in that area. The leaders of the public security station in existence at the time couldn't resolve the problem, which is why it was necessary to appoint an individual who would be able to deal with the matter. At that time, the Croatian population was also maltreated to a certain extent and since an order had been issued according to which any violations of public law and order, and in particular, putting members of others ethnic groups at threat, had to be punished, measures were taken to prevent such acts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have to move back into private session. Or perhaps the beginning of my sentence could be redacted and I will rephrase the question. We can remain in open session but I suggest this be redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, may the sentence -- is that the sentence at page 28, line 7 to 8, that you want to redact?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, that's correct. The beginning of my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. May that sentence then be redacted and may the Chamber please move into private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise. If we redact the beginning of this sentence, it's not necessary to move into private session. We can remain in open session. By redacting the sentence I have referred to we will protect the witness and when rephrasing my question I will make sure that I don't reveal the witness's identity, if you agree to such a procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm in your hands, sir. Thank you very much. Well, we don't have to -- may we stay in open session. Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether Mr. Vujko understood the task he had and the problems that existed, such as you described them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: With regard to the objections to Mr. Vujko and dealing with those problems, do you know whether Mr. Martic was aware of those problems and what was his attitude towards the situation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Mr. Martic wanted to be in control of everything that was taking place in the field, and as a result, he knew what the specific tasks of Mr. Vujko were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what your opinion is? Did Mr. Martic support the steps taken by Mr. Vujko?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Martic really insisted that all citizens in Krajina should be treated on an equal basis. I have said this on a number of occasions. I'll have to repeat this in the future because that is what I believe was the case. In 1992 there was the family Cengic. This happened in the vicinity of Knin. They were victims and everything was done to discover who the perpetrators of the crime were and they wanted to issue a sign to show that such acts could not be committed. The perpetrators were discovered, and criminal reports were filed against them. This is the best example as to how one should proceed if such situations occur.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: To avoid any confusion, I just have one brief question. You said that the Cengic family was killed. There were four members of that family. What was their nationality, and who were the perpetrators, who discovered them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Well, they were Croats, the perpetrators were identified. They were discovered. They were handed over to the district Prosecutor's Office and they were processed by the Knin authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think it's a good time for a break now, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic, you are correct. Court will adjourn and come back at quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, before the break you mentioned the Cengic family, the Croatian family, there were four family members. They were killed and the perpetrators were identified by the Knin SUP. I want to know whether there was a public reaction to that event, to the discovery of the murderers. How did the public react?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I should say that before that event, the Ministry of the Interior made an announcement and said that the Croats had probably committed the act. Their intention was to accuse the Serbian authorities of treating the Croats in Krajina in a certain way. This was the Ministry of Interior's initial approach because such information came from the field. However, having carried out certain investigations, having tried to discover the identity of the perpetrators, they proved that this was not the case, that the initial hypothesis was not valid. They discovered the Serbian perpetrators of the crime, they were arrested, the SUP filed a criminal report, they were handed over to the district court. I think they went to the military court, they were sent to the military court in Banja Luka. As to what happened after that, I don't know. The public was revolted by this murder, and they were relieved when the perpetrators were discovered. As far as I can remember, the main reason for killing the members of that family was looting, they wanted to steal their property, appropriate their property, and as a result they were probably killed. The crime was detected and this demonstrates that the authorities in Krajina acted on the basis of principles and treated all citizens in Krajina in an equal way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Was there any reason why they were sent to a military court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what the justice system was like at the time. The Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia was still in existence then. What's important to me was that the crime was detected, we took all the necessary steps. And I'll emphasise this once more, an announcement was initially made according to which the Croats were the perpetrators, but when we discovered that this was not the case, we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You told us that. I thought you knew the reason for sending them to a military court. I didn't -- these were not prisoners of war, were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In 1992, while you occupied the position you held, as far as you know, were the Secretariats of the Interior -- did the Secretariats of the Interior compile reports? I apologise, my microphone was not on. I'm not sure whether what I said was heard.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: I heard what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The interpreters have heard me. I'm grateful. Were reports filed on their work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Well, the rules were such that reports had to be sent on a daily basis, public security stations had to issue reports on crime to higher level bodies, and they -- and the Secretariats of the Interior would send reports to the Ministry of the Interior, reports that concerned all issues from the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Given the position you held from 1992 to 1994, do you have any information according to which the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska and Krajina assessed the security situation, the criminal situation, the situation as far as law and order was concerned? Was this common practice? Did it take any steps with regard to the situation it came across?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Well, that's an integral part of the work. At the beginning of each year the Ministry of the Interior would draft a working plan for that year, and at the end of the year, they would draft annual reports. This was not just the case for the Ministry of the Interior. All the Secretariats and all public security stations acted in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I ask you to please ask questions, Mr. Milovancevic, don't suggest the answer. That last question suggested the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: For clarification, please, may I ask you, the witness mentioned reports to the Ministry of the Interior. Of what state do you mean? What Ministry of the Interior was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of the Republic of Serb Krajina. I'm talking about the period after the Republic of Serb Krajina was established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: When you told us about killing of the Cengic family, you mentioned some announcement of the Ministry of the Interior that it were probably Croat perpetrators. You remember? What Ministry of the Interior was that? Who gave the announcement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serb Krajina, because the first operative information indicated that, but after this information was checked, this was proved to be false, and then the right information was given out and detection proceeded, and this indicates the principled work of the ministry, because they denied the first false information that it was Croats who had perpetrated the crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. And now, just sorry for the long interruption now, but I got a little lost when you then said their intention was to accuse the Serbian authority of treating the Croats in Krajina in a certain way. Who is "they, their intention was to accuse the Serbian authorities of treating the Croats in Krajina in a certain way"? Whose intention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The communique -- this referred to the Croatian authorities, because the first information was that the Croatian authorities had infiltrated a group on to the territory of the Krajina which had perpetrated this crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Okay. That was part of the announcement, not intention of the author of the announcement? Thank you. Then I understand. And you may continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In connection with this last answer, it might be interesting to ask you the following: You said that the Cengic family was killed. These were Croats. Do you remember how many people were killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: This was a horrific crime, so I remember it. It was a husband, a wife and two children.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In connection with the solving of this crime, do you know what Mr. Martic's attitude was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Mr. Martic was the first or among the first to doubt the reality of the report that this could have been done by Croatian forces, because the area where this happened is deep in the territory near Knin, and for this reason, he insisted that everything be done, that no stone be left unturned, to arrive at the information as to who could have perpetrated this crime. And this was the duty of the Secretariat. The job was completed in a truly professional manner. And the case was solved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the period between 1992 and 1994, and also later on, up to Operation Storm, can you tell us whether you can assess what the circumstances were in which the MUP was active? I'm referring to the policemen tasked with maintaining law and order, traffic control and all other regular police work.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: The situation was extremely difficult because there was a war going on throughout this time. There were quite a large number of Serb members killed. And during the aggression on the Krajina, there was pressure from the general public who wanted the police to make distinctions between crimes perpetrated by Serbs and crimes perpetrated against Serbs. For this reason, it was really difficult for a policeman to do his job, and it was also made more difficult by the fact that people who had military assignments thought that the police was privileged because they didn't have to go to the trenches. This was additional pressure on policemen but they managed to withstand all this pressure. Another problem was the insufficient number of professional staff. This is something we constantly came up against. And for this reason, special plans were drawn up to strengthen the MUP with properly trained professional staff. Assistance was sought from neighbouring countries, from Serbia, but unfortunately, the information was not forthcoming. Some of our staff, however, were trained in Banja Luka, some in Golubic, in the training centre there, and some citizens from the Krajina who had been trained in Belgrade were sought. They were asked to return to the Krajina and work there. So there were many problems which had to be withstood and it was very difficult to work in those circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your response. In 1992, the UN became involved in solving the Yugoslav crisis. Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Of course, because it also impacted on the work of the organisation I belonged to. The Vance Plan was drawn up in early 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, Witness, very briefly, what the main provisions of the Vance-Owen plan were with reference to the Republic of Serb Krajina? What had to be done?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Well, the main thing was that the JNA was to withdraw from the territory of Croatia and Krajina, and four sectors were to be set up, north, south, east and west, and on the territory of the Republic of Serb Krajina, public law and order was to be maintained by the local organs, whereas the CIVPOL forces, which were part of UNPROFOR, would have a monitoring role. They would monitor the work of the local police stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May I interrupt you here? As the question referred to the territory of the Republic of Serb Krajina, can you tell us what was to happen to the Territorial Defence according to the provisions of the Vance-Owen plan, of the Republic of Serb Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: The units were --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Objection. I apologise for the interruption. I've been sort of debating on this as we go along. This is one topic that's as far as I can see and unless I've missed something, is clearly not in the 65 ter summary. As I understand the Rules as of yesterday, I feel obligated to object. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic, any response?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I accept the objection. I was only trying to get an answer to the whole issue, but we have dealt with it sufficiently here, and I will withdraw my question if the Chamber so rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, you have offered to withdraw. There is no need for a ruling. It stays withdrawn. Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the civilian police. Do you know what the attitude of the ministry, or rather, the relationship was between the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serb Krajina and the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: I think that in May or June - I'm not sure of the exact date, but in mid-1992 - the Ministry of the Interior issued written instructions on the relationship between the organs of the Interior of the Republic of Serb Krajina and the CIVPOL.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. And what was the most important part of those instructions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: That the organs of the Interior should do their job independently and fully, that CIVPOL had a monitoring role, that the organs of the Interior should offer their full cooperation to the CIVPOL forces, that the CIVPOL forces had the right to be in the public security stations and monitor the work of the organs, that they had the right to receive complaints from citizens, and that any complaints passed on by the CIVPOL should be received and acted upon, and that cooperation should be as good as possible, and that the work of CIVPOL should not be hindered in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. From the view point of the post you held until the end of the existence of the Republic of Serb Krajina, to the best of your knowledge, were these instructions implemented as regards the attitude towards UNCIVPOL?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: From my point of view, objectively, the instructions were implemented as much as possible. Specifically, once a month we held meetings at sector level attended by the secretaries of the Interior, all the chiefs of the public security stations. These were on the side of the Republic of Serb Krajina. As well as the chief of the civilian police for that sector and all the heads of the monitoring offices. The meetings were held once a month in different locations and at these meetings specific problems were raised which had occurred on the ground. The meetings had two aims. One was mutual respect and the other was to discuss specific issues. And the cooperation was truly successful.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether you had occasion to attend any of those meetings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: I attended all of these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Judging from what was said, or rather, let me put another question first. What representatives of the UNCIVPOL did you personally have occasion to meet at these meetings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: It's hard to remember all their names. Alo Alfie [phoen], I think, was the first head of CIVPOL for Sector South. After that, we had very cordial relations with Mr. Bob Munroe [phoen] from Canada, who was at the head of the civilian police. The relations were not only professional, but in many cases we became very friendly, truly friendly. I feel that this was possible only because they were satisfied with what we were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you felt they were satisfied with what you were doing. What did they tell you about what you were doing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Well, of course, at these meetings, they gave us their views and observations. They said that there had been certain attacks on citizens of the Krajina. And what bothered us a little bit was that it was always Croats they mentioned, and they did not mention crimes against Serbs, which were far more numerous. They drew attention to omissions and failures, and asked that these be corrected in our work, but they also said that they were very satisfied with our work in these difficult circumstances and with the kind of personnel we had at our disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Based on the content of these meetings with the high representatives of the UNCIVPOL, can you tell us, were any objections raised at these meetings with respect to discrimination or criminal attitude toward the Croatian population, for example, intentional neglect to solve these cases?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Well, there is a saying among our people that each person has a different personality and view point. We tried to tell them that every crime was the same, as far as we were concerned, regardless of whether it had been perpetrated against the Serbs or Croats, and that they should view these crimes in the same way, and that if there were failures in the work of the Ministry of the Interior, these were not due to discrimination against the Croatian population but were simply a result of the lack of resources which would enable the immediate detection of the perpetrators of a crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: With respect to the issues you discussed with the representatives of the UNCIVPOL, what do you know about the efforts to solve these crimes and misdemeanours? Did the police do its job properly? Did it try to do its job properly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Well, that's what I've been trying to say all this time. I am proud to say that the police did its very best to do its job properly and correctly, and I can say that we were quite efficient in crime prevention. This is also evident from the number of criminal reports and misdemeanour reports issued by the ministry in the course of a year. I know, for example, with regard to 1992, the Ministry of Justice received over 7.000 criminal reports from the Ministry of the Interior, and many more misdemeanour reports. This indicates the professional work of the police. But whether it's possible to discover all perpetrators, well, I think that's an illusion. It's impossible even today. Here, every day, I hear sirens in The Hague, and in wartime circumstances, everybody tried to go their own way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: May I just --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: This was a little foggy comment on crime prevention and on criminal justice, on criminal police having problems in every country and so on. But were you speaking here of partly very serious incidents, like murder, murder being one of the crimes in general in the world, which is -- which often has a high rate of investigation, finding the perpetrators. So maybe you can give a more specific answer to that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I assume that this is what you have in mind. The police in the Republic of Serbian Krajina treated all crimes as crimes. They tried to discover the perpetrators of the crimes, to solve these crimes. What is disputed and often before this Tribunal is the assessment of some individuals that members of one ethnic group were discriminated against. However, that was not the case. Let me be specific. From the 1st of January 1992 up until about the end of August 1994, I will try to provide a concrete answer to your question. During this period, in the area of Krajina, according to reports from the organs of the Interior, about 570 murders were recorded. That was from the 1st of January 1992 until the end of August 1994. So we are talking about a three-year period. So over 500 murders, of which 60 per cent of those murders were Serbs. The others were members of other peoples, most of whom were Croats. In fact, there were some of them who had remained in the area of Eastern Slavonia. Most of those crimes were solved. When the crimes, when the murders were committed, well, at that time, we knew who the perpetrators were to a significant extent, that about 70 or 80 murders or 60 murders, the perpetrators of which were not known. About 30 per cent of them were discovered when Serbs had been killed and about 30 per cent when Croats were killed. This should demonstrate that the Krajina Police treated all murders in an equal manner, and they acted professionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could we have a look at a document on the screen? It's an UNCIVPOL document. 726 is the Exhibit number. Before it appears on the screen, and to save time, I'll say that this is a document from the civilian police of the UN. It concerns a certain period of time. You'll see which period is concerned when you see the document. You have before you a document, it says the United Nations, John McElligott is the sender, the commissioner's deputy. It was drafted on the 27th of July, 1993. The subject crimes committed against Croats in Sector South. Can you see this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In the first paragraph of the document, it says that they are attaching a report received from UNCIVPOL, Sector South, in which the type and number of crimes committed against the Croats living in Sector South are listed during the period August 1992 until the 31st of May 1993. Men in military or police uniforms are suspected of having committed 120 out of 497 crimes. Can you see the text?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you held the position you occupied, did you ever have the opportunity of examining such a document, of seeing such a document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did UNCIVPOL have the duty of informing the Ministry of the Interior of the situation in the ground -- on the ground and was it their duty to request that certain steps be taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: That's why we had meetings. That was their function. So the answer is yes. But I have never seen such a report. If I can comment on it, I would be glad to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What did you want to say? Is there anything you could say on the basis of such report?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: As far as I can see, this is a report that concerns alleged crimes committed against Croats, against one ethnic group. I'm not sure which number is concerned. But from 1992 to 1994, as I have said, over 7.000 criminal reports were filed, and here they have referred to 497 crimes that were committed. I don't know what they had in mind, what sort of crimes they were concerned with. So this doesn't even represent one per cent of what the MUP in Krajina processed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the second paragraph of this page, it says -- I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: He said MUP in Krajina but this document refers to Sector South. Yeah? Is that the same region? You're speaking of Sector South only? Where the 7.000 criminal proceedings or criminal reports. You were comparing two different things, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, what you have said is quite correct. About 7.000 criminal reports were filed at the level of the MUP, but I think about 2.000 criminal reports were filed in Sector South, but even when we compare this number to the number in the report, well, we can see that that only includes some of the crimes, but I don't know what that's crimes here refer to, whether it concerns looted property or something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The second sentence says -- second paragraph says, "The report might help to demonstrate the fear that exists of how the Knin authorities might act. The contents of the report might also be of interest to the commission for human rights." Given this sentence, what sort of fear is at stake? Why was there fear of what the Knin authorities might do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult to know why such a report was drafted. It's difficult to know the reasons. But given the title, "crimes committed against Croats in Sector South", I assume that the gentleman who is sending the report, the deputy commissioner, was making an allusion to the fact that the Knin authorities weren't doing everything they could to protect the Croatian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, given that this report concerns the period August 1992 to May 1993, given the position you held, perhaps you could answer question as to whether such an illusion is correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: From my view point, from the viewpoint of the position I held, this illusion is not correct. It's not correct in terms of politics either but I will leave this for others to judge. But given the work that I was involved in, these allegations are not correct. Crimes were detected or solved, perpetrators were identified regardless of whether they were Croats or Serbs. Far more crimes committed by Serbs were in fact detected. And I'd also like to point out something else that is of importance. In fact that's quite enough. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is a report from the civilian police of the UN, and you don't agree with it. You're saying that it's incorrect. Did you ever have the opportunity of examining other reports, public reports or UNPROFOR reports, which also alluded to problems on the Serbian side or, rather, accused the Serbian side of having acted in this way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: In the contact that we had, yes, reference was made to the problems that Croats encountered, and on our side we would mention the steps we took. So that was quite sufficient, when it comes to this problem. We have to see which criminal reports were filed and see that the organs of the Interior carried out their duties to the extent that that was possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In August 1992 to May 1993, when this report was compiled, Mr. Martic was the Minister of the Interior of the Republic of Serbian Krajina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether UNCIVPOL representatives had any contact with Mr. Martic and were such issues raised with him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the discussions were about, what was Mr. Martic's position when it came to resolving crime, whatever the nature of the crime was? And I'm referring to the contact he had with UNCIVPOL.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Well, I do know what was discussed. I do know what his position was because Mr. Martic addressed the issue at meetings and when he addressed the public. But I also know this from the contact I had with UNCIVPOL representatives. They said that Mr. Martic insisted on resolving all crimes, especially crimes committed against Croats, and I also know that at one meeting with Mr. Thornberry in 1993, in May or June, this issue was also discussed and Mr. Martic said that everything was being done to resolve all crimes, and in particular, crimes committed against Croats. Many citizens in Krajina were disturbed by this because they said, you're interested in crimes committed against Croats and not crimes committed against Serbs, who were in the majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You've provided us with two important pieces of information. Firstly, you said that UNCIVPOL representatives informed you personally of Mr. Martic's position; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And the second important piece of information is that the local Serbian population even objected to the fact that he was more interested in solving crimes committed against Croats, whereas there were Serbs who were victims too?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Yes. They didn't just object to him. They objected to us when we performed our duties, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And these objections raised by the civilian population, did they obstruct you? Did they make you cease your activities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We no longer need this document on the screen. Could the usher please distribute a document to my colleagues from the Prosecution and to the Chamber as well as to the witness? We have a sufficient number of copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If I might inquire, Your Honours, if this was on the list of documents that we received from Defence counsel or if it -- if it has a 65 ter number or an exhibit number or some other thing or is this the first time right now that I see this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this document isn't on the Prosecution's list, it doesn't have a 65 ter number. This document -- well, this is the first time the document has been seen in the proceedings. This is a Defence document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, we got no notice that this was going to be used. It's the first time I lay eyes on this document. Until I have a chance to review it, I guess I don't know if I object to it but I object to the procedure by which during the course of examination I receive a document for the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am sorry that I have just heard this. I informed my Defence team that they should inform my colleagues from the Prosecution about the document. They should provide them with the document. We translated it or had it translated and we've made a certain number of copies, not to hide the document. But to be able to district copies to everyone. I'm surprised by the fact that my colleagues haven't been provided with copies. Perhaps I can check and see what has actually happened at the next session, but I really don't have all the information right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We understand that but then what do we do at this stage? Obviously you can't use the document if you didn't give an advance copy to your opposite number. That's the problem. You can check during the break, but what do we do now?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in that case, we won't use the document right now. I'm taken by surprise too. I have to check and see what happened. There was some sort of misunderstanding in the Defence team, I assume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't want to cause any problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. Then we may proceed on the next point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, a minute ago you said that you had direct contact with UNCIVPOL representatives, and they even told you about Mr. Martic's position to how one should act. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could one say, given your experience, given the knowledge that you have, that in the territory of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, the authorities, and that includes the MUP of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, systematically and deliberately terrorised and persecuted the Croatian population because they were Croatian. Was there such a systematic campaign of terror in the Republic of Serbian Krajina, given the experience you had and the position you held, can you answer that question?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: That certainly is not the case. Had that been the case, I wouldn't have performed the duties that I performed. And what was done in the field confirms what I am saying, what was done in the field during that period of time. What is important to underline is the fact that most of the murders, and there were more Serbs who were murdered than Croats, but most of the murders of Croats took place at the demarcation line, which in 1992 was under the JNA. That's an area where the organs of the Interior were not able to perform their duties. We are talking about villages at the very demarcation line, and for certain reasons, or rather, because of the wartime situation, such situations did occur. It's important to establish that in the interior of Krajina, where I worked, apart from the murder that I have mentioned in 1992, in Knin, there was no other murder of Croats. And this should also demonstrate how all the citizens of the Republic of Serbian Krajina were treated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, from the standpoint of your work experience, who was part of the MUP of the Republic of Serb Krajina? I'm referring to the kinds of -- I'm trying to avoid putting a leading question so let me stop there. Who made up the MUP? What forces conditionally speaking? What people? What employees made up the MUP?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: If you're talking about 1992 --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: In 1992, in accordance with the Vance Plan, from early 1992 and in mid-1992, the MUP of the Republic of Serb Krajina was composed of the public security administration and the state security administration, as well as special purpose police units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. With respect to these special purpose police units that were mentioned, do you know when and where they were established?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: The special purpose police units were established in accordance with Vance Plan, because according to that plan, the JNA was to withdraw and the separation lines or the demarcation lines with Croatia were to be secured by the police. Pursuant to, I think, a decision issued by the Federal Secretariat of National Defence of the Yugoslav Secretariat, special purpose units were established in the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly, if I say that according to you, the special purpose units were in fact the border police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Yes. They had the competence to secure the borders, and make sure there were no terrorist incursions, and therefore, they were armed pursuant to the Vance-Owen plan. I'm not a military expert but I think it was up to 12.7 calibre, other weapons, heavy weapons, were stored in depots under the double control of the UN, the UNPROFOR and the local forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us or did I understand you correctly, which organ issued the decision on establishing these special purpose units? Did you mention that a while ago? I missed it, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: I'm certain that the decision was made pursuant to a decision of the Federal Secretariat of National Defence of the Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia, with the purpose of filling the void created by the departure of the JNA and for purposes of implementing the Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In accordance with what you said I'm interested in another thing. Do you know whether according to the Vance Plan, UNPROFOR had the duty of securing the demarcation line between the Republic of Croatia and the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: No. It didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I think the question before was not answered. Wasn't it a question, Mr. Milovancevic, by whom the decision was made to establish the special purpose units?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it seemed to me that I understood the answer, but I will put the question to the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Once again, Witness, please, do you know who or what organ, what institution, issued the decision on establishing the special purpose police units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: What I know for certain is that the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was a signatory and guarantor of the Vance Plan, and that pursuant to the withdrawal of the forces of the JNA, which according to that plan were to withdraw from the Croatian Krajina, it issued a decision. I don't know what organ exactly issued this decision, but these decisions were then to be deployed within the Ministry of the Interior of the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm getting confused now when the witness says he doesn't know who issued the decision because he told us at page 50, lines 22 to 25, that I'm certain that the decision was made pursuant to a decision of the Federal Secretariat of National Defence of the Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia with the purpose of filling the void created by the departure of the JNA and for purposes of implementing the Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: So it wasn't said by whom but just pursuant to a federal decision, but then we would like to know how it happened, what was going on then, in the Krajina itself, and here you don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I continue with my questions and I believe that Your Honours will get the answer. We will take a look at a document and things will become much clearer. Your Honour, are you -- do you agree with what I have just suggested?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Could we please take a look at document -- the 65 ter document 1334? It's dated the 28th of April 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. -- oh, --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. Unless I'm getting my signals crossed with Defence counsel, this also is not on the list of documents that I was provided. It's 65 ter number 1334? Am I correct? I don't want to make a mistake about this and press an issue that's not actually there, but otherwise yet again it's a document that I wasn't notified about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it should be, because there are two or three documents which are very important to us. I even know the number off by heart, 1334 and 1367. These are documents we must have informed our learned friends about. These are documents that have already been used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Check if you have proof of delivery to them because it doesn't help to say "we must have." Just say we did on such and such a date. Here is proof.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Maybe the number is just wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And while you're dealing with that, may I just remind you, Mr. Milovancevic, when you check the previous document, you will find that the English translation of the previous document is only three pages, whereas the Serb document is nine pages, and has a conclusion by way of date and signature. And the English translation seems to be just stopping in the middle. In addition, the English translation seems to be having things that are skipped because you keep getting three dots in a bracket which you don't get in the Serb, B/C/S original. Just check all those things so that when you do come back to that document, if you intend to do so, you give -- you make sure that you give us a complete document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in connection with the document that, the translation of which you mentioned last, the document has nine pages. We don't need all nine pages. We only need the parts we translated and marked. And this will be adduced in evidence when the time comes. That's why only part of the document was translated. But of course, the entire nine-page document in B/C/S was provided. If our learned friends need to use the whole document of course they can do that, but we are using only parts of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: They may very well want to use that, Mr. Milovancevic, for them to get the context of the three pages maybe they need to get the nine pages. If you can just give a full document, please, without skipping some paragraphs. But that's not for discussion now. I've asked you what to do with that. Let's deal with this one. This one on the screen, again, there is an objection that the Prosecution haven't received it. Are you finding your proof of delivery to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if this document on the monitor is marked 1334, then I mistook the number. It's not the document I was intending to show. This is something entirely different and my learned friend is quite right. I must have made a mistake in the number. It's the SSNO order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just get the correct one, Mr. Milovancevic. That's fine. Thank you. Let's go to the correct document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just one more question for the Registry. Is this document 1334, the one on the screen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes, this seems so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will deal with this document after the break, the document I was intending to show. And now I will ask to see another document, in order not to waste time. It's 1367 from the Prosecutor's list.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you see before you on the monitor this document, witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Would you read the heading to us and what it says in the corner?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: "Republic of Serbian Krajina, Main Staff of the Serb army, date and number 947, 23/1, the title is the reforming of the Territorial Defence and the special purpose units of the police into the Serb army of the Republic of Serb Krajina."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we proceed, I'll ask you the following: Do you know what forces made up the special police units? You said that they were established pursuant to a decision made by the authorities in Belgrade. We'll look at that document later. But what was the strength of these units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, there were supposed to be eight brigades and about 16.000 men, but I also know that not all these brigades were formed, and that about four units received flags, but the units for Eastern Slavonia, Western Slavonia and I don't know what others were not actually established. So only four came into existence. The others were formed only when the Serb army of the Republic of Serb Krajina was formed, and I also know that these special police units were under the administration of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us in what period the special police units existed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: As of April 1992, until this date, the 27th of November 1992, when, pursuant to agreement with international community, they were reformed to make up the Serb army of the Republic of Serb Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: If I may only add, as regards dates, I ask Their Honours to bear in mind that it's very hard to remember some things. It's very hard to be like a robot and simply remember things that happened so long ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
